title: Argenx to buy peptide platform in potentially billion-dollar deal
content: An article from Dive Brief Argenx to buy peptide platform in potentially billion-dollar deal For $550 million up front, Argenx will take control of Unnatural Products’ “macrocyclic peptide” technology and direct it to develop oral, durable medicines for serious immune-mediated diseases. Published Nov. 9, 2026 Jacob Bell Lead Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Argenx agreed to acquire Unnatural Products, a maker of "macrocyclic peptides," on Nov. 9, 2026. deliormanli via Getty Images Dive Brief: Argenx, a Netherlands-based biotechnology company focused on antibody drugs, on Monday said it has agreed to acquire a protein specialist in a potentially billion-dollar-plus deal. Unnatural Products has a platform that pairs machine learning, screening and other techniques to engineer “macrocyclic peptides.” These peptides are larger and more complex than typical small molecules, which allows them to more effectively bind to tricky proteins and address some challenging diseases. Yet, they’re still tiny enough that they can be swallowed. Argenx plans to use the platform to develop oral, durable medicines for serious immune-mediated diseases. The acquisition carries a $550 million upfront cash payment. Unnatural Products could receive up to $595 million more if specific milestones are hit. if (!$(selector).closest('.pf-comments__ad-wrapper').hasClass('borders')) { $(selector).closest('.pf-comments__ad-wrapper').addClass('borders') } } }); } }); }); Dive Insight: Unnatural Products claims macrocyclic peptides hold the potential to unlock targets once thought to be “undruggable.” That premise, along with the California company’s technology platform, proved enticing to both venture capitalists and big-name pharmaceutical firms like Merck & Co. and Novartis. Argenx was drawn in as well, having already taken a minority stake in Unnatural Products before pursuing a full buyout. In a statement, Argenx CEO Karen Massey said these macrocyclic peptide capabilities are “highly complementary” to her own company’s antibody engineering. “After working together for more than two years, we also know there is a strong fit in how we work: science first, entrepreneurial and focused on patients,” Massey added. “We want to preserve what has made [Unnatural Products] successful while bringing the strengths of both teams together.” The Food and Drug Administration has already approved at least a handful of macrocyclic peptide therapies. In 2020, for example, Rhythm Pharmaceuticals’ Imcivree was cleared as a treatment for certain genetic forms of obesity. The following year, Aurinia Pharmaceuticals’ Lupkynis became the first-ever oral medicine for adults with active lupus nephritis. In 2023, the FDA greenlit a UCB medicine called Zilbrysq for “generalized myasthenia gravis,” a rare autoimmune condition that’s become somewhat of a battleground for several developers. Argenx’s own flagship product, Vyvgart, targets this disease and brought in $4.5 billion in net product sales from January through the end of September. Thomas Smith, a Leerink Partners analyst who covers Argenx, wrote in a note to clients that the new acquisition “represents potential for longer-term strategic value.” He explained there’s a desire — both in big pharma and in the broader immunology and inflammation research space — to make oral, long-acting therapeutics that are able to be more effective and convenient than conventional biologics. The Unnatural Products deal, which comes on the heels of Argenx’s potentially $2.2 billion purchase of Forte Biosciences, also “signals further focus on pipeline growth and diversification,” Smith wrote. Shares of Argenx were up nearly 3% by late Monday morning, to hover around $953 apiece. Add us on Google Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Filed Under: Deals

title: AstraZeneca Acquires Omniose, Adding Bioconjugation Platform to Vaccine Pipeline
content: Advertisement News|Articles|November 10, 2026 AstraZeneca Acquires Omniose, Adding Bioconjugation Platform to Vaccine Pipeline Author(s)Nicholas Jacobus Key Takeaways Omniose will be absorbed into AstraZeneca’s Infectious Disease Unit, bringing in-platform bioconjugation capabilities to augment AstraZeneca’s preclinical vaccine pipeline; deal terms were not disclosed. Traditional chemical conjugation can yield heterogeneous products, challenging characterization and release testing, while risking epitope modification; bioconjugation enables intracellular antigen–carrier linkage for improved control. Glycoconjugate vaccines have reduced morbidity and mortality from Hib, pneumococcus, meningococcus, and typhoid, with secondary antimicrobial-resistance benefits via lowered antibiotic utilization. External validation includes GSK’s Shigella (Phase IIb) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (Phase I) programs and Janssen/J&J’s ExPEC nine-serotype vaccine advanced to Phase III. Strategic emphasis centers on leveraging differentiated conjugate engineering to advance vaccines against serious bacterial infections increasingly complicated by antimicrobial resistance.SHOW MORE AstraZeneca acquires Omniose, to bolster it's preclinical infectious disease programs. Advertisement AstraZeneca has entered a deal to acquire Omniose, following a three-year exclusive research collaboration between the two organizations that both sides described as productive.Christian Harding, CSO and co-founder of Omniose, frames the acquisition as the culmination of years of partnership. “This milestone reflects the work of exceptional and complementary teams,” Harding says. “AstraZeneca has been a trusted partner for several years, and this acquisition gives our platform the best chance to reach the patients it was built to serve.”¹Under the terms of the agreement, Omniose is set to become a wholly owned subsidiary of AstraZeneca and will join the company’s Infectious Disease Unit.¹ The deal brings Omniose’s proprietary bioconjugation platform and expertise into AstraZeneca, complementing the larger company’s existing capabilities and supporting its preclinical vaccine programs.¹ Financial details of the deal have yet to be disclosed.What problem does bioconjugation solve?Conventional conjugate vaccine manufacturing requires chemical cross-linking of bacterial polysaccharide antigens to immunogenic carrier proteins, a process that is complex and makes the resulting vaccines difficult to produce reproducibly and to characterize, requiring extensive release testing before use.2 The non-specific nature of that cross-linking, and the conditions chemical conjugation requires, can also lead to undesired modifications of epitopes that may affect the quality of the immune response generated against the polysaccharide antigen.2 Bioconjugation offers what is described as an elegantly simple alternative to chemical conjugation, producing and linking the antigen and carrier protein within a single cell.2 (()=>{var l=(n,t)=>{let Merck KGaAWhy does this technology matter for public health?Polysaccharide conjugate, or glycoconjugate, vaccines have already proven enormously successful at reducing disease and death from infections caused by bacterial pathogens including Haemophilus influenzae type B, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Salmonella typhi.2 These vaccines carry an added public health benefit by preventing the infections they target, while also helping to fight antimicrobial resistance by reducing the overall use of antibiotics.2The underlying bioconjugation science has already moved through clinical development in other hands. Omniose co-founder Mario Feldman provided the work leading to the industrialization of bioconjugate vaccine technologies by GSK, following that company’s acquisition of GlycoVaxyn/Limmatech’s bioconjugate platform technology, for vaccine candidates against Shigella, which is now in Phase IIB development, and Klebsiella pneumoniae, now in Phase I development.2Janssen, now known as Johnson & Johnson Innovative Medicine, separately licensed the same underlying platform to develop a bioconjugate vaccine against extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli targeting nine serotypes, advancing that candidate into Phase III development.2Benjamin Moutier, senior vice president, infectious disease, AstraZeneca, points to the scientific differentiation Omniose’s platform offers. “Omniose’s bioconjugation platform represents a differentiated approach to engineering conjugate vaccines and strengthens our ability to develop novel vaccines against serious bacterial infections,” Moutier says. “Building on the strong scientific collaboration between our teams, we look forward to advancing these programs and realizing the potential of this technology for patients.”What comes next for the combined vaccine programs?With the acquisition complete, Omniose’s bioconjugation platform now sits inside AstraZeneca’s Infectious Disease Unit, where it is positioned to support the unit’s existing preclinical vaccine programs targeting serious bacterial infections.1Timothy Cooke, CEO of Omniose, describes the acquisition as a shared win built around a common mission. “The acquisition by AstraZeneca is a great outcome for both organizations,” Cooke says. “We share a vision for bringing the best science and talent together to address serious bacterial infections, which are increasingly complicated by antimicrobial resistance.”SourcesOmniose Announces Its Acquisition by AstraZeneca Omniose November 10, 2026 title: AstraZeneca buys vaccine startup; FDA issues GLP-1 safety warning
content: An article from News roundup AstraZeneca buys vaccine startup; FDA issues GLP-1 safety warning The deal gives AstraZeneca a simpler way to make conjugate vaccines. Elsewhere, a psychedelic depression drug was submitted to the FDA and an autoimmune disease-focused biotech’s shares collapsed. Published Nov. 11, 2026 By BioPharma Dive staff Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Today, a brief rundown of news involving AstraZeneca and the Food and Drug Administration, as well as updates from Compass Pathways, Zura Bio and Abeona Therapeutics that you may have missed. AstraZeneca has acquired vaccine startup and development partner Omniose. The two companies didn't disclose deal terms in their announcement Tuesday. But the transaction hands AstraZeneca "bioconjugation" technology, a more efficient way to make the conjugate vaccines that strap a protein to an immune system-provoking antigen. Omniose claimed the technology could yield "higher-quality" conjugate vaccines. AstraZeneca intends to use the approach to make shots for serious bacterial infections. if (!$(selector).closest('.pf-comments__ad-wrapper').hasClass('borders')) { $(selector).closest('.pf-comments__ad-wrapper').addClass('borders') } } }); } }); }); The Food and Drug Administration has called for the prescribing information for widely popular GLP-1 therapies to be updated to include the possible risk of contracting a rare condition that causes vision loss. The FDA began investigating the issue following case reports of GLP-1 recipients developing "non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy," or "NAION." A review of animal data failed to uncover why GLP-1 drugs might be associated with NAION, but a meta-analysis of many trials found a higher rate of cases in treatment recipients. NAION's been seen with every marketed GLP-1 drug, too, the FDA said. The agency, as a result, believes there is a “potential increased risk of rare NAION events,” it said Monday. — Ben Fidler Compass Pathways said Monday it has completed an approval application in the U.S. for a synthetic psilocybin drug it calls “COMP360” and that it’s developed for treatment-resistant depression. In clinical testing, six weeks of treatment with COMP360 was associated with, on average, a 3.8-point reduction on a 60-point scale measuring the severity of depression symptoms. The drug is part of a wave of research into psychedelic medicines and could receive a particularly speedy review following the company’s receipt of a special Food and Drug Administration voucher. — Jonathan Gardner Shares of Zura Bio plunged by more than two-thirds on Monday following the company’s announcement that its lead product missed the main goal of a Phase 2 trial in people with the autoimmune skin condition hidradenitis suppurativa. Neither of two tested doses of the dual-pronged antibody drug tibulizumab significantly reduced the number of abscesses and inflammatory nodules in enrollees after 16 weeks, nor were secondary trial goals met. Zura will halt development in hidradenitis suppurativa, but continue studying tibulizumab in other immune diseases. Per deal terms, Abeona issued Ellodi $20 million worth of shares, and promised to pay Ellodi another $60 million should its drug win FDA approval and hit certain sales milestones. Abeona raised $30 million in a private share sale alongside the deal. Previously called APT-1011 and now ABO-801, the drug is an oral form of the steroid fluticasone that dissolves in the mouth and is delivered directly to the esophagus. — Jonathan Gardner Add us on Google Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Filed Under: Biotech
